opus-5.5.text:
I think it could matter quite a lot, though maybe not in the way people first expect.

Right now, a huge fraction of training cost is really the cost of ignorance. We don't fully understand why a given architecture works, why a certain learning rate schedule helps, why loss spikes happen, or when a model is actually learning a new skill versus just memorizing. So what do we do? We run massive sweeps, we try many configurations, we scale up and hope. A lot of compute goes into what I'd call blind search.

If we have a physics-like understanding of AI, meaning we can identify the right "macroscopic variables" and the laws that govern them, the way thermodynamics lets you reason about a gas without tracking every molecule, then a lot of that search can be replaced by prediction. Scaling laws are already a first, rough example. Once people realized loss follows a fairly smooth power law in compute, data, and parameters, you could train small models and extrapolate, instead of gambling on a giant run. That alone saved enormous amounts of money. I think there's much more of that waiting to be discovered.

Let me give a few concrete directions. One is training dynamics. Phenomena like grokking, where a model suddenly generalizes long after it has fit the training data, or the edge-of-stability behavior in optimization, tell us that training goes through phases. If we understand those phases, we can design optimizers or schedules that skip the slow, wasteful parts. In some of our work on grokking, once we understood it in terms of representation learning and the scale of the weights, we could make it happen much faster, sometimes by orders of magnitude, just by controlling the right quantity.

Another is representation. If we understand how models internally structure knowledge, for example through superposition, where features are packed into more dimensions than they nominally have, then we can reason about how big a model actually needs to be for a given task, and maybe why scaling laws have the exponents they have. That tells you where you're wasting parameters.

A third is architecture. When you understand the principles, you can build in the right inductive biases instead of having the model rediscover them from data at great cost. That was part of the motivation behind things like Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks: asking whether there are more natural building blocks that make some kinds of structure, especially scientific structure, cheaper to learn.

That said, I want to be honest about the limits. Understanding doesn't automatically mean cheaper in total. Historically, when something becomes more efficient, people just use more of it. So the cost per unit of capability will likely go down, but total spending might still go up, because people will want to push the frontier. And physics of AI is still quite young. We have a lot of phenomenology, interesting observations, toy models, but not yet a unified theory. It's a bit like physics before Newton, or thermodynamics before statistical mechanics.

But I'm optimistic. In the history of engineering, the big leaps in efficiency usually came after understanding. Steam engines got dramatically better once thermodynamics was understood. I think AI is in that steam-engine moment right now: it works incredibly well, but we don't fully know why. Clarifying the physics is how we go from brute force to design.

r001.rationale: The response says understanding training dynamics could enable better optimizers and schedules that skip slow, wasteful parts of training, reducing compute costs.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it could go either way in the short term, but in the long run I'm fairly optimistic it brings costs down, and I'll try to explain why.

Right now, a lot of what we do in training large models is closer to alchemy than to chemistry. We have scaling laws, we have a bag of tricks that empirically work, but we often don't know why they work, or when they'll stop working. So the way the field makes progress is by running enormous experiments. You try a new architecture, a new optimizer, a new data mix, and you find out by burning a lot of compute. That's expensive, and a huge fraction of that spend is essentially trial and error.

What I mean by the "physics of AI" is trying to find the underlying principles, the simple laws that govern how these systems learn. Things like: why do models grok a concept suddenly instead of gradually? What determines the exponent in a scaling law? Why does a particular loss landscape have the geometry it does? If we understood those things the way a physicist understands, say, thermodynamics, then we could predict outcomes before running the experiment. You'd be able to say, this architecture will plateau at this point, or this data mixture is wasteful because the model is spending capacity on something it can't actually use.

That's where the cost savings come in. Prediction replaces search. In physics, once you have a theory, you don't need to build a thousand bridges to figure out which one stands. You compute it. Right now in AI, we're still building the thousand bridges.

I'd also add that understanding usually reveals waste. When you look inside these models with the tools of mechanistic interpretability or just careful toy models, you often find that a lot of the parameters and compute are doing something surprisingly simple, or redundant, or just noise. If you can characterize that, you can design models that are much leaner for the same capability. Some of my own work on alternatives to standard architectures was motivated exactly by that, the idea that if you understand what structure the function has, you can build the inductive bias in rather than paying for the model to discover it from scratch.

Now, the caveat. Science is slow, and it's not free. Doing this research well sometimes means running very controlled experiments that don't produce a product, and from a company's point of view that can look like a cost without an immediate return. So in the near term, clarifying the physics might actually require spending more, not less, on things that don't look like frontier training runs.

But I think of it like the difference between compounding returns and linear returns. Scaling gives you linear returns on dollars spent. Understanding gives you something that keeps paying out every time anyone trains a model afterwards. So my bet is that the field, and especially the labs that can afford to be patient, will find that a little bit of physics goes a very long way.

r001.rationale: The response says understanding AI’s underlying principles can replace costly trial and error with prediction, identify wasteful data mixes, and enable leaner models—explaining how training can be optimized to reduce costs.

astra-6.text:
I think it could make training much cheaper by helping us understand which parts of the computation are actually necessary. Right now, we rely heavily on trial and error: we try different architectures, learning rates, and data mixtures, and then run expensive experiments to see what works. If we had a better theory of how models learn, we could make those choices more systematically.

There’s also a more fundamental question: how much computation does learning a particular task really require, and how far are our current methods from that limit? Clarifying the physics of AI could help us distinguish unavoidable costs from inefficiencies in our algorithms. I wouldn’t promise a particular reduction yet, but that’s the opportunity: using understanding to replace some of the brute-force search.

r001.rationale: The response says a better theory could guide training choices more systematically and distinguish algorithmic inefficiencies from unavoidable costs, identifying opportunities to improve current methods and reduce training costs.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main benefit would be making training less dependent on trial and error. Today, we spend a lot of compute trying different architectures, learning rates, and data mixtures without fully understanding why one choice works better than another. If we had better principles for how learning happens, we could rule out many unsuccessful experiments before running them.

That could also help us understand when a larger model or more training data is actually necessary, and when a better design could achieve the same result with less computation. But understanding alone doesn’t automatically reduce costs—we would need to turn those insights into practical training methods. So I see clarifying the physics of AI as a path toward more predictable and efficient training, rather than a guarantee that training suddenly becomes cheap.

r001.rationale: The response says better principles could eliminate unsuccessful experiments and guide designs that achieve the same results with less computation, describing practical ways to optimize training methods.
